title: Tendinopathy and loading
goal: Describe the tendinopathy continuum and its critics, and compare eccentric, heavy slow resistance and isometric loading with an honest view of the evidence.

steps.title: Tendinopathy: load-driven tendon pain
steps.text:
A [tendon](g:tendon) joins muscle to bone and carries the load of every stride and pedal stroke. [Tendinopathy](g:tendinopathy) is pain and poor function in a tendon, brought on by load. The Achilles tendon (back of the heel) and the patellar tendon (below the kneecap) are the two most studied [[c:it-common]].

It is hard to treat because people present so differently. Older descriptions called it degenerative or failed healing; neither fits every case. People of different ages and loads show varying pain, irritability and ability to function [[c:it-heterogeneous]].

claims.text: Achilles and patellar tendinopathy are overuse injuries that are common among athletes.

evidence.quote: Achilles and patellar tendinopathy are overuse injuries that are common among athletes.

claims.text: Tendinopathy looks different from person to person: neither the degenerative nor the failed-healing description explains all presentations.

evidence.quote: The pathology of tendinopathy has been described as degenerative or failed healing. Neither of these descriptions fully explains the heterogeneity of presentation.

steps.title: The continuum model, and its critics
steps.text:
In 2009 Cook and Purdam proposed a continuum of tendon pathology: tendons sit at different points between early, reversible change and long-standing change, and treatment should fit the point. Some tendons recover with simple interventions; some resist everything [[c:it-cont]].

The first stage is the reactive tendon: pain after sudden overload. There, the tendon can regain normal structure with optimal management, and heavy eccentric exercise may be highly provocative [[c:it-reactive]].

But staging by structure is questioned, because tendinopathy is mainly a pain condition.

claims.text: The continuum model places tendons on a range of pathology and aims to match treatment to the stage; recovery is variable.

evidence.quote: This review proposes, and provides evidence for, a continuum of pathology.
Recovery is similarly variable; some tendons recover with simple interventions, some remain resistant to all treatments.

claims.text: In the reactive stage, a tendon can regain normal structure with optimal management, and heavy-load eccentric exercise may be provocative and harmful.

evidence.quote: it remains possible for the tendon to regain its normal structure with optimal management.
Notably, heavy load eccentric exercises or intratendinous injections may be highly provocative and deleterious within this reactive stage.

debate.question: Should tendinopathy be staged by tendon structure?

sides.position: Yes, in part: a continuum of structure guides which treatment to pick.
Doubtful: classifying by structure in what is mainly a pain condition has been challenged; structure, pain and function are not yet linked clearly.

steps.title: Eccentric loading: the old standard
steps.text:
For years the standard conservative treatment was isolated [eccentric](g:eccentric) training: slowly lowering a load, such as a heel drop for the Achilles tendon. It became the dominant approach, yet in some cases up to 45% of patients may not respond [[c:it-ecc-use]].

When a review compared loading programmes, it found limited (Achilles) and conflicting (patellar) evidence that eccentric loading beats other programmes [[c:it-ecc-evid]]. That questions how firmly it became the default.

claims.text: Isolated eccentric training became the dominant conservative treatment for Achilles and patellar tendinopathy, but up to 45% of patients may not respond.

evidence.quote: Isolated eccentric muscle training has become the dominant conservative management strategy for Achilles and patellar tendinopathy but, in some cases, up to 45 % of patients may not respond.

claims.text: Evidence that eccentric loading beats other loading programmes is limited for the Achilles and conflicting for the patellar tendon.

evidence.quote: This review has identified limited (Achilles) and conflicting (patellar) evidence that clinical outcomes are superior with eccentric loading compared with other loading programmes, questioning the currently entrenched clinical approach to these injuries.

steps.title: Heavy slow resistance
steps.text:
[Heavy slow resistance](g:heavy-slow-resistance) (HSR) loads the tendon with heavy lifts, raised and lowered slowly. In a trial of 58 patients with chronic Achilles tendinopathy, 12 weeks of HSR or eccentric training improved function and pain equally, and the gains held at 52 weeks [[c:it-beyer]].

What differed was sticking to it: compliance was 92% with HSR and 78% with eccentric training. Satisfaction at 12 weeks tended to favour HSR (100% against 80%, P = .052).

For the patellar tendon, the review found greater evidence for HSR [[c:it-patellar]].

claims.text: HSR and eccentric training gave equal clinical gains in Achilles tendinopathy; HSR had better compliance (92% vs 78%).

evidence.quote: None of these robust clinical and structural improvements differed between the ECC and HSR groups.
the mean training session compliance rate was 78% in the ECC group and 92% in the HSR group, with a significant difference between groups (P < .005).

claims.text: For patellar tendinopathy there was greater evidence for HSR loading than for isolated eccentric loading.

evidence.quote: There is equivalent evidence for Silbernagel combined (Achilles) and greater evidence for HSR loading (patellar).

steps.title: What makes loading work, and isometrics
steps.text:
Why does loading help? The only mechanism consistently linked to better outcomes in both tendons was better muscle performance: torque, work, endurance [[c:it-mech-claim]]. In the Achilles, scan changes (thinner tendon, less blood-flow signal) mostly did not track clinical outcome (a majority of studies, including all high-quality ones).

So scans are a poor scoreboard for rehab; strength and function are better.

[Isometric](g:isometric-contraction) holds may ease pain quickly. In 6 volleyball players with patellar tendinopathy, one bout cut single-leg decline-squat pain from 7.0 to 0.17 out of 10, lasting at least 45 min [[c:it-iso]]. It is a pain relief tool, not proof of healing.

claims.text: Better muscle performance was the only mechanism consistently linked to clinical improvement in Achilles and patellar rehabilitation; imaging change mostly did not track Achilles outcome.

evidence.quote: The only potential mechanism that was consistently associated with improved clinical outcomes in both Achilles and patellar tendon rehabilitation was improved neuromuscular performance (e.g. torque, work, endurance)

In the Achilles tendon, a majority of studies did not find an association between improved imaging (e.g. reduced anteroposterior diameter, proportion of tendons with Doppler signal) and clinical outcomes, including all high-quality studies.

claims.text: One bout of isometric contractions cut patellar tendon pain for at least 45 minutes in 6 volleyball players.

evidence.quote: A single resistance training bout of isometric contractions reduced tendon pain immediately for at least 45 min postintervention and increased MVIC.

points: Tendinopathy is load-driven tendon pain; the Achilles and patellar tendons are the main sites.
The continuum model sets tendons on a range, but staging by structure is contested because pain and structure do not match.
Eccentric training was the standard, but evidence that it beats other loading is limited or conflicting.
HSR matched eccentric training in the Achilles trial with better compliance; muscle performance, not scan change, tracks recovery; isometrics ease pain in the short term.

options.text: A tendon rupture that needs surgery
options.why: A rupture is a tear; tendinopathy is a load-driven pain condition.

options.text: Load-driven pain and poor function in a tendon
options.why: Right: a pain condition brought on by load.

options.text: Inflammation that always shows clearly on a scan
options.why: Scans do not always match pain, and the old inflammation idea does not fit every case.

options.text: A muscle strain that has spread into the tendon
options.why: It is a tendon problem in its own right, not a spread-out muscle strain.

variants.stem: A runner adds a block of hill repeats and gets pain at the back of the heel, worse in the first steps after rest. Which tendon is most likely involved?

options.text: Achilles tendon
options.why: Right: the Achilles tendon runs down the back of the heel.

options.text: Patellar tendon
options.why: The patellar tendon sits below the kneecap.

options.text: Quadriceps tendon above the knee
options.why: That is higher up the leg, nowhere near the heel.

options.text: Plantar fascia under the foot
options.why: A different structure, under the foot rather than at the back of the heel.

variants.stem: A volleyball player has pain just below the kneecap that worsens with jumping. Which tendon is most likely involved?

options.text: Achilles tendon
options.why: The Achilles tendon is at the back of the heel.

options.text: Patellar tendon
options.why: Right: the patellar tendon sits just below the kneecap.

options.text: Hamstring tendon behind the knee
options.why: That is behind the knee, not below the kneecap.

options.text: Iliotibial band at the hip
options.why: A different structure, at the outside of the hip and knee.

variants.stem: A triathlete adds track intervals and feels pain in the tendon at the back of the ankle. Which tendon is most likely involved?

options.text: Patellar tendon
options.why: The patellar tendon is at the knee.

options.text: Tibialis anterior tendon at the front of the ankle
options.why: That is the front of the ankle, not the back.

options.text: Achilles tendon
options.why: Right: the Achilles tendon is the large tendon at the back of the ankle.

options.text: Quadriceps tendon above the knee
options.why: That is higher up the leg.

variants.stem: What does the continuum model of tendon pathology say?

options.text: Tendons are either healthy or degenerate, with nothing in between
options.why: The model is the opposite: a range of states.

options.text: Pain level alone tells you the stage of the tendon
options.why: Pain and structure are not the same thing; the model uses structural change.

options.text: Every tendinopathy ends in rupture if not treated
options.why: The model does not predict rupture; some tendons recover simply.

options.text: Tendons sit at different points on a range, so treatment should fit the point
options.why: Right: early changes differ from long-standing ones.

variants.stem: A runner doubles her hill work in a week and her Achilles gets sore for the first time. A friend says to start daily heavy heel drops. What does the full text of the review suggest?

options.text: Start at once: heavy eccentrics are the cure at every stage
options.why: In the reactive stage they may be highly provocative and deleterious.

options.text: Be careful: in a reactive tendon, heavy eccentric work may flare it
options.why: Right: settle the load first; this stage can recover with good management.

options.text: Stop all load for six months, as the tendon cannot recover
options.why: The reactive tendon can regain normal structure, and the text does not say to stop all load.

options.text: Get an injection first, as it works best early
options.why: Injections are named as possibly provocative in the reactive stage.

variants.stem: A scan shows disorganised tendon structure in a pain-free runner. Which reading fits the 2016 critique of the continuum?

options.text: Structure and pain are not tightly linked, so a scan alone should not decide treatment
options.why: Right: tendinopathy is mainly a pain condition.

options.text: She is certain to develop pain soon, so start treatment now
options.why: The critique says structure does not map neatly onto pain.

options.text: The scan is wrong, because disorganised tendon always hurts
options.why: Structure and pain can differ; the scan may be right.

options.text: Structure is irrelevant, so ignore scans in every case
options.why: The authors still see use in structure; they call for linking it with pain and function.

variants.stem: About what share of patients may not respond to isolated eccentric training?

options.text: Up to 5%
options.why: Far too small; non-response is a real problem.

options.text: Up to 15%
options.why: Too low; the review reports a higher figure.

options.text: Up to 45%
options.why: Right: in some cases, up to 45% may not respond.

options.text: Up to 80%
options.why: Too high; most trials show gains for many patients.

variants.stem: In the Achilles trial, HSR and eccentric training improved function equally. Compliance was 92% with HSR and 78% with eccentric. Satisfaction was 100% against 80% (P = .052). Best reading?

options.text: HSR is clearly better, since satisfaction was 100%
options.why: The satisfaction gap was not statistically clear (P = .052); outcomes were equal.

options.text: Eccentric training is better, since it is the older method
options.why: Age of a method says nothing about results; outcomes were equal.

options.text: Equal results: HSR was easier to stick to, so a fair first choice
options.why: Right: no outcome difference, better compliance, a non-clear satisfaction gap.

options.text: Compliance proves HSR heals tendons faster
options.why: Compliance was higher, but healing was no faster: outcomes did not differ.

variants.stem: For patellar tendinopathy, what did the review find about HSR and eccentric loading?

options.text: Greater evidence for HSR, conflicting evidence that eccentric is better
options.why: Right: HSR had greater evidence in the patellar tendon.

options.text: Clear proof that eccentric beats every other programme
options.why: The evidence for eccentric superiority was conflicting.

options.text: No loading programme had any evidence at all
options.why: Several loading programmes were compared; they had evidence.

options.text: Only isometric holds were studied
options.why: The review compared eccentric, combined and HSR programmes.

variants.stem: After 12 weeks of loading, a runner's Achilles looks unchanged on ultrasound, yet she is pain-free and stronger. What does the review suggest?

options.text: The programme failed, because the scan did not change
options.why: In most Achilles studies, scan change did not track clinical outcome.

options.text: Her strength is irrelevant to the pain relief
options.why: Better muscle performance was the mechanism linked to improvement.

options.text: The scan must be wrong, since pain-free tendons look normal
options.why: Scans and symptoms often differ; the scan is not necessarily wrong.

options.text: This is plausible: clinical gains often come without scan change
options.why: Right: muscle performance tracked outcomes; imaging mostly did not.

variants.stem: One bout of isometric holds cut pain from 7.0 to 0.17 in 6 players. What is the main limit when reading this?

options.text: Only 6 players and one bout: it shows short-term relief, not healing
options.why: Right: tiny sample, one session, 45 minutes of follow-up.

options.text: A crossover design cannot test pain
options.why: Crossover designs can test pain; each player acts as their own control.

options.text: Volleyball players are too fit to represent anyone
options.why: Fitness matters less than the tiny sample and the very short follow-up.

options.text: A fall from 7.0 to 0.17 is too large to be real
options.why: Large effects can be real; the problem is the size and length of the study.
